findings.title: async forEach callback breaks error handling and ordering
findings.body: bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...}) is wrapped in a try/catch, but forEach does not await the async callbacks. Previously (sync code) a thrown error inside the callback would propagate synchronously and be caught by the surrounding try/catch. Now that the callback is async and awaits getCalendar(), any error thrown inside becomes a rejected Promise that is never awaited, so it escapes the try/catch entirely and becomes an unhandled promise rejection instead of being logged via logger.error. The function also returns before all deletions settle, so callers relying on completion (e.g. before sending reschedule emails) might run concurrently with/ahead of the pending deletions.

findings.title: Same unhandled-rejection issue as vital/reschedule.ts
findings.body: Identical pattern: bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...}) inside a try/catch. Making the callback async while using forEach means thrown/rejected errors from getCalendar()/deleteEvent() bypass the try/catch, resulting in silent/unhandled promise rejections rather than being logged.

findings.title: forEach with async callback not awaited for calendar/video cleanup before sending reschedule emails
findings.body: bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... }) is fire-and-forget: the surrounding code (sendRequestRescheduleEmail, webhook dispatch) proceeds without waiting for these calendar/video deletions to finish or to catch their failures. Converting getCalendar to async made this race more pronounced, since previously the deletion happened synchronously or near-synchronously; now it's an unawaited microtask chain and any failures are swallowed as unhandled rejections.

findings.title: Dynamic import() calls are still evaluated eagerly, not actually lazy
findings.body: Each `import("./app")` call in the object literal executes immediately when this module is evaluated (as soon as `appStore` is imported anywhere), regardless of whether a given app is ever used. Simply storing the resulting Promise instead of awaiting it does not defer the module loading/bundling — bundlers like webpack will still create and request each chunk at the time this file runs. This negates the stated goal of the PR (async/lazy imports of app-store packages) while adding async/await overhead to every call site that previously did synchronous property access, with no actual reduction in initial load work for consumers who only need one app.

findings.title: getCalendarCredentials still treats getCalendar as returning a value directly used downstream without documenting it's now a Promise
findings.body: `const calendar = getCalendar(credential);` now stores a Promise<Calendar|null> in the `calendar` field of the returned structure (relying on later code awaiting `item.calendar`). This is a subtle API shape change (every consumer of getCalendarCredentials() must know to await `.calendar`) that is not documented via types/comments, making it easy for a future caller to accidentally treat it as a resolved Calendar object.

findings.title: Nested async forEach for recurring-event calendar deletions remains unawaited
findings.body: `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` pushes into apiDeletes asynchronously inside a forEach that isn't awaited by the enclosing code before `apiDeletes` is used in `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))`. If the outer `if (bookingCalendarReference)` block finishes and the function moves on before these async pushes complete, some deletions could be missed from apiDeletes, resulting in orphaned calendar events in that recurring-event + allRemainingBookings branch.
